title: Hold On to Your Kids
author: Gordon Neufeld and Gabor Maté
theme: Children grow best when their deepest attachment is to the caring adults in their lives, and parents must actively protect that bond so that peers do not replace them as a child's main guide.
takeaway: This week, greet your child each morning and after school with warm eye contact, a smile and a few unhurried minutes of attention before giving any instructions or reminders.
summary: Gordon Neufeld, a developmental psychologist, and Gabor Maté, a physician, argue that something important has shifted in modern childhood. More and more children look to other children, rather than to parents and teachers, for direction, values and a sense of who they are. The authors call this peer orientation, and they see it as a quiet cause of many family struggles.

Their central point is that attachment comes before everything else. A child who feels close to a parent naturally wants to follow, please and learn from that parent. When the main bond moves to friends, parents lose their natural authority, and no amount of rewards, threats or rules can fully make up for it.

The authors link peer orientation to problems such as defiance, bullying, a need to fit in at any cost, and children who seem to stop caring. Peers cannot offer the unconditional acceptance that young people need, so many children protect themselves by shutting down their softer feelings. This, they suggest, can stall real emotional growth.

The good news is that parents can win their children back. The book describes collecting a child: catching their eye, offering warmth, and inviting them to depend on you before asking anything of them. Busy schedules, separations and screens all compete for a child's attention, so parents are encouraged to bridge time apart, protect family meals and rituals, and keep adults like grandparents and teachers close.

Discipline, too, should protect the relationship. The authors caution against punishments that use separation or withdrawal of love, because these weaken the very bond that makes children cooperative. Instead, parents are urged to stay calm, connect first, and steer behaviour through the strength of the relationship. In their view, a child who feels safely held at home is free to grow into a confident, independent person.

questions.q: What do the authors mean by 'peer orientation'?
options: Children learning to share toys with friends
A school programme that pairs older and younger pupils
Children looking to other children, rather than adults, for direction and values
Parents asking other parents for advice
questions.why: Peer orientation is the shift of a child's main attachment and guidance from adults to peers.

questions.q: According to the book, what gives parents their natural authority?
options: A strong attachment between parent and child
A clear system of rewards and punishments
Being stricter than other parents
Earning more money than the child's friends
questions.why: The authors argue that a child who feels attached naturally wants to follow and learn from the parent.

questions.q: Why, in the authors' view, can't peers properly replace parents?
options: Peers are always badly behaved
Peers live too far away
Peers are too busy with homework
Peers cannot offer the unconditional acceptance a child needs
questions.why: Children's acceptance of one another is changeable, so it cannot provide the security that adult care gives.

questions.q: How do many peer-oriented children protect themselves from hurt, according to the book?
options: By talking to their parents more often
By shutting down their softer, more vulnerable feelings
By becoming more dependent on teachers
By spending more time alone reading
questions.why: The authors describe children numbing their tender feelings to cope with the insecurity of peer relationships.

options: Picking them up from school on time
Gathering their belongings at the end of the day
Catching their eye, offering warmth and inviting them to depend on you
Collecting rewards for good behaviour
questions.why: Collecting is the friendly act of re-establishing connection before making any demands.

questions.q: What should parents do before asking a child to do something, according to the book?
options: Connect with the child first
Offer a reward in advance
Remind them of the last punishment
Give a written list of rules
questions.why: The authors stress that connection should come before direction.

questions.q: Why do the authors caution against discipline that uses separation, such as withdrawing love?
options: It takes too much time
It weakens the very bond that makes children cooperative
It is too gentle to work
It makes children too dependent
questions.why: Punishments based on separation threaten the attachment that underlies a child's willingness to follow.

questions.q: Which practice does the book encourage to strengthen family attachment?
options: Cancelling all family meals to allow more study
Letting friends decide weekend plans
Giving children unlimited screen time
Protecting shared rituals such as family meals
questions.why: Rituals like eating together give children regular, reliable moments of connection.

questions.q: What role do grandparents and teachers play in the authors' view?
options: They can form a wider circle of caring adults around the child
They should stay out of a child's life
They should replace parents entirely
They are only useful for homework help
questions.why: The authors encourage keeping other caring adults close so the child's attachments point toward grown-ups.

questions.q: What do the authors believe a securely attached child will eventually become?
options: Permanently dependent on parents
Unable to make friends
A confident, independent person
Uninterested in learning
questions.why: They argue that secure attachment at home is the foundation for healthy independence.
